content.text: {"relation": "DIVERGENT", "consensus_summary": "All four blind responses converge: 'Gospel' (euangelion) is the good news of salvation accomplished in Jesus Christ's death for sins, burial, and resurrection (1 Cor 15:1-4; Rom 1:16), with a widely recognized complementary emphasis on the announcement of God's kingdom (Mark 1:14-15) and a secondary literary sense (the four canonical books). Kingdom-, liberation-, and Isaianic-restoration readings are treated as accents within the same core, not replacements of it.", "book_summary": "The book identifies the Gospel as 'the gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion,' citing Isa 52:7, Isa 2:3, Jer 31:33, and Heb 4:2. Its common-view note explicitly flags the death-burial-resurrection definition as the view 'commonly taught,' which it sets aside in favor of a covenant/Torah-from-Zion identification: the good news is God's reign and the writing of His law on hearts under the renewed covenant.", "consensus_core_identification": "The Gospel = the proclamation that God has saved humanity through Christ's atoning death and resurrection (with the kingdom's arrival as an integrated emphasis).", "book_core_identification": "The Gospel = the gospel of the kingdom, concretely identified as the renewed covenant and the law going forth from Zion (God reigns; His law is internalized in His people).", "core_relation": "CONTRADICTS", "extension_relation": "PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION", "boundary_disagreement": "The book retains the kingdom-proclamation cases the consensus admits (Mark 1:14-15-type texts, Isa 52:7's 'Thy God reigneth'), and via Heb 4:2 extends the gospel backward to pre-Christian Israel, but it displaces the consensus's defining content — Christ's death and resurrection — from the center and reclassifies the gospel's substance as covenant/law (Isa 2:3; Jer 31:33), a content the consensus never identifies with the gospel itself.", "material_contradiction": "The consensus defines the gospel's content as the accomplished saving events of Christ's death and resurrection (1 Cor 15:1-4 as the standard defining text). The book's common-view note explicitly quarantines that definition as merely 'commonly taught' and instead identifies the gospel as the renewed covenant / the law going forth from Zion. Identifying the gospel's core with law and covenant rather than with the cross-resurrection kerygma cannot be true simultaneously with the consensus's identification in the same sense; accepting the book requires replacing the consensus's central referent, not merely re-weighting emphases. This is sharpened by the fact that mainstream (especially Pauline) theology typically contrasts gospel with law.", "rationale": "The book does not simply adopt the kingdom-emphasis alternative the consensus lists as 'common'; that alternative still treats the kingdom announcement as centered on Christ's saving work and God's reign, not as identical with Torah/covenant. By explicitly marking the death-burial-resurrection definition as the common view it corrects, and by defining the gospel as 'the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion,' the book replaces the consensus identification with a law/covenant referent found in no consensus response except, faintly, Response B's minority 'new law or ethical system' alternative — and even that concerns Jesus' teachings (Sermon on the Mount), not Zion-Torah and Jer 31:33 covenant renewal. The cores materially contradict even though extensions partially overlap (kingdom proclamation texts), so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED is correct.", "citation_support": "PARTIAL", "strongest_objection": "One could argue REFINED: the consensus itself lists 'the gospel of the kingdom' as a common alternative reading, and the book's phrase leads with exactly that; Jer 31:33's new covenant is also arguably contained within mainstream gospel theology (Christ's blood inaugurating the new covenant), so the book might be seen as a covenantal sharpening of an admitted alternative rather than a replacement. Additionally, Heb 4:2 genuinely shows biblical usage of 'gospel' preached before Christ's death, lending some textual footing to a definition not anchored in the cross-resurrection events.", "confidence": "medium"}
